title: After the Echo

content: {"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Ameen, a 14-year-old boy, walked alone through a crooked lane, clutching his red doll as the sky wept in a woeful rhythm. At last, he entered his home and picked up a pen half-filled with blue ink to write a letter to his beloved mom and dad. His love for them was still evident in the opening of the letter, where he addressed his mother as \"Ummi...\" Yet he knew they had been killed in a missile strike that had hit like lightning, unlike his younger sister, who still waited for their return, hoping they would bring her sweets."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Soon, Ameen felt a burning hunger in his stomach, so he went with his sister to the refugee camp and ate a hearty meal. Afterward, he began crafting sculptures out of clay and painted them as soon as they were finished. His blue eyes shimmered with tears, carrying a torrid tide of both grief and joy. When he completed the sculptures of his mom and dad, he fixed his blue eyes upon them, unable to look away. Later, he walked to his neighbour's house. As he was running, a piercing alarm echoed from the refugee camp. The moment its sound crashed into his ears, he sprinted back as fast as he could and grabbed his beloved sister. Even then, he carefully carried the clay figures of his parents with him."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Later, he took them out and handed them to his sister. While she was playing with them, a sudden rain of missiles descended upon them. The air itself felt like a ticking time bomb before the explosions began. In that instant, his mind flashed back to the night he had lost his mom and dad—the night his dreams took flight, the night hope slipped through his fingers, the night he lost everything. And now, at last, he was going to be happy, for he believed he would be reunited with them. Perhaps these fiery ripples would grant him and his sister a second chance to live with the family they had lost."}]}]}

Importance of the Islamic Medieval Period"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The Islamic Medieval period, also known as the Islamic Golden Age, 8th to 13th centuries CE, was a classical era in the history of Islam. Now, let's delve into the inspiring epistemic models that took place in the Islamic Golden Age, the classic period."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","marks":[{"type":"bold"}],"text":"5.1 Institutionalization of Knowledge: The Medieval Framework"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The Qur’anic worldview led to a civilization structured around learning. Educational facilities increased across the famous regions. Bayt-Al-Hikma, the House of Wisdom, established in the 9th century in Baghdad under Caliph Al Mamūn, became a center for translation and scientific research. It was one of the famous research centers that improved the studies of the scholars who learned and worked there. Bayt-Al-Hikma was essentially the world's first research institute. It laid the foundation for systematic"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"scientific inquiry and cross-cultural scholarship. It mainly served as a library, translation center, and academy. The Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit books were translated into Arabic, including the works of Aristotle, Plato, and Galen. The Mu'tazilite school of theology, supported by Al-Ma'mūn, encouraged science and philosophy. Famous scholars like Al-Khawarizmi and Al-Kindi studied and worked there, which led to the innovations of algebra and algorithmic calculations from there. The invention of astronomical tables and refinements in celestial measurement was finished from there. In medicine, the scholars, for the first time, experimented and tested models from there, creating the first systematic medical encyclopedias in Arabic. Consequently, Bayt-Al-Hikma became a hub of astronomy, science, mathematics, and medicine in this era. The second famous research center during the Medieval period was the Dar-Al-Hikma, founded in 1005 CE by the Fatimid Caliph Al Hakim Ibn Amr Allah in Cairo, Egypt. It contained one of the largest libraries of the medieval world, along with its function as a research institute. It became an inspired model for later madrasas and universities, enlightening a culture of open access and scholarly patronage, and influencing educational methods like lectures, public debates, libraries, and research grants. Science, philosophy, and astronomy were taught by salaried professors, in parallel with theology and Qur’anic exegesis, which functioned as a learning system where students learn all the subjects synthesized with the Qur’an. Furthermore, the use of logic ("},{"type":"text","marks":[{"type":"italic"}],"text":"'ilm al-manṭiq"},{"type":"text","text":") was developed and completed from here. In essence, this dual focus on the Qur’an and scientific-philosophical thoughts created scholars who saw science as a path to understanding God's creation and strengthening faith, not a contradiction of faith. This system was active both in Bayt-Al-Hikma and Dar-Al-Hikma. In addition to these two, there were also other famous research centers developed in the Medieval Age. They include Al-Azhar University, one of the longest continuously operating universities in the world, and the Al-Andalus research centers, active in Cordoba, Granada, and Toledo. Some other active observatories were the Damascus observatory in Syria, the Maragha observatory and Shammasiyyah observatory in Iran, the Ulugh Beg observatory in Samarkand, and the Taqi al Din's observatory in Istanbul. In the final analysis, the observatories and research centers played a crucial role in constructing knowledge harmonized with the Holy Qur’an. They helped bring about the rise of prominent scholars who strongly believed in their religion and spread an empowering message to society: that preventing the influence of secular thought on religion by denying science is not the right way. title: Commercialization of Education: Opportunities and the Oppression of Knowledge Production
excerpt: The commercialization of education has transformed learning into a market-driven enterprise, creating both unprecedented opportunities and significant challenges for knowledge production. While private investment, technological innovation, global competition, and institutional efficiency have expanded access to education and improved infrastructure, commercialization has also intensified inequality, commodified learning, weakened academic freedom, and redirected research toward market interests. This essay critically examines the dual nature of educational commercialization by exploring its economic, social, and epistemological dimensions. It argues that although market mechanisms can enhance educational quality and accessibility, excessive commercialization undermines the public purpose of education and restricts the production of independent, socially relevant knowledge.
content: {"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Education has historically been regarded as a public good that nurtures intellectual development, democratic citizenship, social mobility, and cultural continuity. Universities and schools have served as institutions where knowledge is created, preserved, and disseminated for the collective benefit of society. However, the expansion of neoliberal economic policies since the late twentieth century has transformed education into an increasingly market-oriented enterprise. Educational institutions now compete for students as consumers, private corporations participate actively in curriculum design and educational technology, and research agendas are often influenced by commercial interests. This process, commonly referred to as the commercialization of education, has fundamentally reshaped the purpose, governance, and outcomes of educational systems worldwide."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commercialization does not merely involve the privatization of educational institutions. This transformation has generated both opportunities and profound concerns. On one hand, commercialization has expanded educational access through private investment, encouraged innovation, promoted technological advancement, and improved institutional efficiency. On the other hand, it has commodified learning, intensified educational inequality, marginalized critical inquiry, and subordinated knowledge production to corporate and economic interests."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This essay critically examines the commercialization of education by exploring both its opportunities and its implications for the oppression of knowledge production. Students gain exposure to different perspectives, while universities benefit financially from international tuition fees and expanded academic networks."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Global competition has encouraged institutions to improve educational standards and align curricula with international benchmarks."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commercialization and the Oppression of Knowledge Production"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Despite these advantages, commercialization has generated serious concerns regarding the nature and purpose of knowledge production."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":3},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commodification of Knowledge"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Perhaps the most significant consequence of commercialization is the commodification of knowledge. Education increasingly emphasizes economic returns rather than intellectual development or social transformation. Knowledge becomes valuable primarily when it generates profit, enhances employability, or contributes to economic competitiveness."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Consequently, humanities, philosophy, history, literature, sociology, and the arts often receive reduced funding compared to business, engineering, information technology, and medical sciences."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The narrowing of academic priorities limits intellectual diversity and weakens critical thinking."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":3},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Corporate Influence on Research Agendas"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commercial funding significantly shapes contemporary research priorities. Research addressing poverty, social justice, environmental sustainability, indigenous knowledge, or public welfare may receive comparatively less support because it offers limited financial returns."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Such funding structures create conflicts of interest and compromise academic independence. Research productivity often becomes more important than intellectual originality or long-term scholarly inquiry."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"This \"publish or perish\" culture encourages quantity over quality and discourages critical, interdisciplinary, or controversial research that may not produce immediate measurable outcomes."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Academic freedom becomes constrained when institutional priorities align more closely with financial sustainability than intellectual independence."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":3},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Educational Inequality"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commercialization frequently reinforces social inequality. High tuition fees at private institutions create barriers for economically disadvantaged students. Although scholarships exist, access to prestigious educational institutions often depends upon financial resources."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The emergence of elite private schools and universities creates a stratified educational landscape where wealth influences educational quality, career opportunities, and social mobility."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commercial coaching centers further widen inequalities by providing competitive examination preparation primarily to students who can afford expensive services."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Education thereby shifts from being an equalizing force to reproducing existing social and economic inequalities."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":3},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Standardization and Market Metrics"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commercialization encourages standardization through rankings, accreditation systems, performance indicators, and employability statistics."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Universities increasingly compete for global rankings, often emphasizing publication counts, citation indices, international student enrollment, and graduate salaries."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"While these indicators provide useful benchmarks, they cannot adequately measure educational quality, ethical development, civic engagement, or intellectual creativity."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Standardization pressures institutions to prioritize measurable outcomes over deeper educational values."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Knowledge production becomes increasingly driven by performance metrics rather than genuine intellectual exploration."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":3},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Marginalization of Critical Knowledge"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Market-oriented education tends to privilege disciplines that directly contribute to economic growth while marginalizing critical and transformative scholarship."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Critical theories examining colonialism, capitalism, gender inequality, environmental justice, and structural discrimination may receive limited institutional support because they challenge dominant economic and political interests."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Similarly, indigenous knowledge systems, local cultural traditions, and community-based research often remain underrepresented within commercial educational models."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The commercialization of education therefore contributes to epistemic inequality by privileging certain forms of knowledge while excluding others."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commercialization in the Digital Era"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The rise of digital education has intensified commercialization. Educational technology companies increasingly influence curriculum design, assessment methods, student data management, and instructional delivery."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and personalized educational platforms offer significant pedagogical benefits. However, they also generate concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, surveillance, and corporate control over educational infrastructure."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null}},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Digital commercialization thus extends beyond financial transactions to include ownership and control over educational data and knowledge infrastructures."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Balancing Market Efficiency with Public Responsibility"}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Commercialization should not be understood solely as either beneficial or harmful. Rather, its consequences depend upon institutional governance, regulatory frameworks, and societal priorities."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Governments retain an essential responsibility to ensure equitable access to quality education through sustained public investment. Public universities require adequate funding to preserve academic freedom and support independent research."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Policies promoting transparency in corporate research partnerships, protecting academic autonomy, regulating tuition fees, and supporting marginalized disciplines are necessary to maintain educational integrity."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Universities should balance market responsiveness with their broader social responsibilities by promoting interdisciplinary research, ethical scholarship, community engagement, and democratic participation."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Knowledge production must remain guided not only by economic value but also by human welfare, environmental sustainability, social justice, and cultural preservation."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"textAlign":null,"level":2}},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The commercialization of education represents one of the defining transformations of contemporary educational systems. It has expanded access, stimulated innovation, strengthened industry collaboration, and contributed to institutional modernization. These developments have enabled educational systems to respond more effectively to technological change and global economic competition."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"."}]},{"type":"paragraph","attrs":{"textAlign":null},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Education cannot be reduced to a commercial enterprise without compromising its democratic, intellectual, and social purposes. Universities and schools must remain spaces where knowledge is pursued not only for economic gain but also for the advancement of human understanding, ethical reflection, cultural diversity, and social justice. Achieving a balanced educational system requires integrating the efficiencies of market mechanisms with a firm commitment to education as a public good. Only through such balance can societies ensure that commercialization serves educational development without oppressing the independent production of knowledge."}]}]}

title: Mental Health Awareness Among Youth
excerpt: Mental health is important for the well-being and success of young people. Youth face stress from studies, family, social expectations, and technology. Awareness helps them understand their feelings and seek support. Schools, families, and society should provide care, remove stigma, and promote healthy habits for better mental health.
